messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar has spent most of his forty-one years building things that last—concrete foundations, steel frames, structures meant to withstand the elements. His own internal world, however, feels precarious, assembled from fragments of a childhood he cannot escape. The trauma is not a single event but the atmosphere he breathed for years: the sound of his father’s voice rising in anger, the sight of his mother shrinking away. He remembers one night in particular, not as a continuous film, but as a series of stark, silent photographs in his mind. The first is his father’s face, contorted with rage. The next is a shattered glass on the floor. The last is the impassive, uniformed presence of the police officers who arrived long after the shouting had stopped, their authority a symbol of help that came too late. This is why, decades later, the sight of a police car can still make his heart pound against his ribs, a visceral, physical reaction that seems to come from nowhere.

These triggers are woven into the fabric of his daily life. At the construction site, a disagreement with the foreman over a delayed shipment sends a jolt of alarm through him. The confrontation, no matter how minor, feels loaded with imminent danger. This sense of threat immediately brings forth those photographic flashes from his childhood—his father's furious eyes, the glint of broken glass. The memory isn’t something he chooses to recall; in fact, when he tries to deliberately piece together the sequence of events from that night, he finds the narrative dissolves, leaving only those same, searing images. The clarity of these fragments makes the world feel intensely unsafe, a place where violence can erupt without warning. He finds himself constantly scanning his coworkers’ faces, searching their expressions and body language for the first sign of a threat, a tightening jaw or a narrowed eye that tells him to brace for impact.

The intrusive nature of these memories and the constant feeling of being under siege have shaped how Omar copes. When the foreman presses him for an answer about the delayed materials, Omar feels the familiar surge of panic. To escape it, he retreats inward, drifting off into a world of his own where the noise of the work site fades and he is somewhere else entirely, somewhere quiet. This mental escape has become his primary defense. The more the memories intrude, the more he relies on this fantasy world or dwells on a vague, safer time before he understood what the shouting in his house meant. This constant retreat, however, only makes him more sensitive to triggers. By avoiding any potential conflict, he has become hyper-attuned to the possibility of it, and by dwelling on the past, he keeps the memories fresh and potent, ensuring they are always close to the surface, ready to be activated.

This cycle has tightened its grip over the years. A trigger, like his boss asking to discuss future project timelines, induces a state of high alert. The very idea of the future feels fraudulent, a promise of stability that was broken long ago. This feeling of threat then pushes him to withdraw, to avoid the conversation, perhaps by claiming he needs to check on something urgent. This avoidance, in turn, validates his belief that the world is dangerous and that he is not equipped to handle it. His strategy of mentally escaping has consequences; his foreman has warned him about his tendency to "zone out," interpreting it as carelessness. The more he retreats into fantasy to manage his fear, the more he scans for threats in the world around him, and the more readily those photographic memories surface, confirming his deepest conviction: that he is fundamentally unsafe.

He came to therapy because his foreman gave him a final warning. His job, the one place where he felt a sense of solid, tangible accomplishment, is now at risk. He is single, with few close friends, his avoidance of conflict having eroded relationships over the decades. He feels trapped in a loop, where the memories fuel the threat, the threat fuels the avoidance, and the avoidance ensures the memories never lose their power. Omar’s greatest hope is to one day be able to talk about the future—a week, a month, a year from now—and feel something other than a cold dread. His fear, whispered in the first session, is that the boy who watched his family shatter is all he will ever be, and that he will never be able to build a life of his own that feels truly safe.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explain that the trauma memory itself makes Omar more sensitive to or aware of triggers.
